paras: The shooting of Dink Batsel took place on the night of April 8, 1882, in Stringtown, a Black neighborhood of Dallas, Texas, when Police Officer Charles Clapp shot Batsel, a Black man wanted for burglary, while trying to arrest him. Clapp said he fired because he mistook a soda-water bottle in Batsel's hand for a pistol, and the wound was thought to be mortal, but Batsel escaped wounded into the brush. No report of his death was found.

According to the Dallas Herald, Batsel, also printed as "Dink Batzelle" and "Dick Batsell," was wanted in both Dallas and Sherman for burglaries. The paper charged him with taking jewelry from Mrs. Carleton's residence, which was later recovered from a pawn-shop, and a Dallas telegram said the authorities had been watching for him for several weeks.

About 9 o'clock that night Clapp and Officer Ed Cornwall came upon Batsel in a dark part of the "negro quarters," and he ran for the brush. The officers overtook him, and when he resisted arrest Clapp struck him over the head with a pistol and knocked him down. As Batsel rose he struck at Clapp with a soda-water bottle, which the officer, seeing it gleam in the dark, took for a pistol, and Clapp fired on him with a large Colt's pistol.

Batsel staggered and fell, then got up and made his way into the dense brush, crawling part of the time on his hands and knees. The officers searched with lights but could not find him, and the Herald reported that the search would resume in the morning.

No later report of Batsel's death, capture or an inquest appears in the coverage. In May the Waco Examiner listed two jail cases of "State vs. Dink Batsel" on the district court docket for June 1, 1882, but nothing in the item ties that defendant to the Dallas shooting.

The story ran first as a special telegram from Dallas in the Waco Daily Examiner of April 9, which called Batsel "a noorious [notorious] and desperate negro burghar [burglar]" and described the wound as "supposed to be a mortal wound." The Dallas Weekly Herald gave the fullest account on April 13 under the heading "A Burglar Shot," naming the second officer and the escape into the brush. The same day the Las Vegas Daily Gazette in New Mexico printed the Dallas telegram word for word under the headline "Dead Dink," with a dateline of April 12, although its text said only that the wound was supposed to be fatal.

Each report told the story from the officers' side, treating the burglary charges as settled and presenting the mistaken bottle as the reason Clapp fired. No account from Batsel or any other witness appears in the reports.
The Las Vegas printing dated the shooting April 12, but the Waco telegram dated April 8 had already appeared on April 9, so the earlier date is better supported.

reader.title: Shooting of Dink Batsel
bases: Dallas police officers shot a Black man wanted for burglary while trying to arrest him; no crowd or mob is mentioned (A1, A2).

A Waco special telegram (A1, reprinted with a later dateline in A3) and a separate local Dallas Herald item (A2) agree on the officer, the victim, the attempted arrest, the soda-water bottle and the shooting, though both appear to rest on the officers' account.

accounts.label: Dallas wire telegram
accounts.gist: Clapp found Batsel in a dark part of the negro quarter; Batsel resisted with a soda-water bottle that Clapp mistook for a pistol, and Clapp fired, inflicting a wound supposed mortal or fatal.

accounts.label: Dallas Herald local report
accounts.gist: Batsel ran for the brush when he saw the officers; Clapp and Cornwall overtook him, Clapp struck him over the head with a pistol, Batsel rose and struck at him with a soda-water bottle, and Clapp fired; Batsel crawled into the brush and escaped the search.

framing.detail: The Dallas Herald headed it 'A Burglar Shot', presented the officer's mistake about the bottle as the reason for firing, and listed the burglaries charged to Batsel.

The Waco Examiner and the Las Vegas Gazette ran the same telegram calling him 'a notorious and desperate negro burglar'; the Gazette headed it 'Dead Dink' though the text said only that the wound was supposed fatal.

conflicts.note: The Waco printing appeared on April 9 and the Dallas Herald's weekly of April 13 reprints a local item saying 'last night', so April 8 is the better-supported date; the April 12 dateline appears to be a re-dating of the old telegram.
Spelling varies; all describe the same shooting.

versions.value: Wound thought mortal; escaped into the brush, not found

conflicts.note: No report of his death was found; a Waco docket entry for a 'Dink Batsel' in June 1882 (A4) may indicate he survived, if the same man.

acts.note: Officers chased Batsel, who ran for the brush, in an attempt to arrest him.
Clapp struck him over the head with a pistol, knocking him down, when he resisted arrest.
Clapp fired a Colt's pistol, said to have mistaken a soda-water bottle for a pistol; wound supposed mortal.
Officers searched with lights for the wounded man in the brush; not found.
